Today's business world seems to be getting ever more competitive, litigious and fast-paced - the maritime industry is no exception. Given the changing climate for day-to-day activities, it is not surprising that business ethics are continually tested. This week saw the passing of a legend in the shipping industry, Morris Louis Feder. Mr. Feder touched the lives of many, as a friend and a mentor, and continuously exhibited several of the qualities - honesty, integrity, and fairness - that can sometimes be lost in the quest to make the next dollar.

Morris got a job as a longshoreman. One day on the docks he met a landsman from Shanghai who recognized Morris as the man who had helped so many to find their way to freedom and safety. This man told Morris that he would help him leave the grueling work on the docks to a position in the front office of the shipping company. Who could have known that from that humble start, Morris would raise himself to the very top of the maritime shipping world and make friends and colleagues all over the world as he did?
In 1950 after a couple of years of hard work, Morris and Lucy finally had saved enough to be married in Brooklyn. They were devoted to each other. With Morris working extremely long hours to make it in the shipping business, it was left to Lucy to manage affairs at home. Morris and Lucy were blessed with two children, Harry and Karen.
When Karen was a young girl, they were away on a vacation. Morris was on the phone much of the time. Karen complained that her father was always so engrossed in his work. Lucy explained to her that this was his job and that because he did his job so well they had enough money to take nice vacations. So when her father finally got off the phone and rejoined his relaxing family, Karen told him to go make another call.
During Harry's and Karen's childhood Morris traveled frequently and worked long hours. Harry remembers that whenever one of Morris' ships was in a nearby port, whether it was New York, Brooklyn, Newark or Philadelphia, his dad would take him along to see the ship. The family even went on cruises on the Freighter, which was a thrill eating at the captain's table and seeing the inner workings of the maritime world.
Once Harry and Karen grew older, Lucy accompanied Morris on many of his business trips. She was a remarkable asset, charming business associates and placing foreign customers at ease. Together they were an unstoppable team.
In 1991, after 43 years of extraordinary leadership, Morris Feder retired as the Executive Vice President and Director for the Maritime Overseas Corporation.

Morris was acting as the United States government's negotiator with Russia over shipping the very large wheat deal. This past June, Morris was honored at the Silver Bell Awards Dinner. The Silver Bell Award is presented by the Seaman's Church Institute to recognize an outstanding individual's, company's or organization's commitment to merchant mariners and the issues facing the maritime industry.
At the dinner, Morris L. Feder received a Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of his distinguished service to the maritime industry, as a respected international negotiator and a businessman of integrity as well as for his dedication to human dignity and the promises of globalization...
There can be no doubt what a towering giant Morris was in the maritime industry, but it was more than that. He was beloved by those he worked with. They trusted and respected this remarkable man.
In recent years he worked as a consultant in the shipping business. He even enjoyed investing in a number of Broadway shows...
When Lucy passed away in 1998, Morris's heart was surely broken. After all, they had shared so much over the years: enormous sadness and ineffable joy.
Morris never stopped being a devoted "grampa" to Jean, Laura, Ali and Emi. Living around the corner from Ali and Emi, he was able to share in so much of their lives. As a father-in-law to Gilli and Ross, Morris was a person they could always count on.
In this Feder family, there will be graduations and weddings in the coming months and years, and yes, Morris will be with you at these sacred milestones.
In conclusion, surely Walt Whitman's poem can help us mourn our "Skipper."
O Captain! my Captain! our fearful trip is done; The ship has weather'd every rack, the prize we sought is won; The port is near, the bells I hear, the people all exulting, While follow eyes the steady keel, the vessel grim and daring: But O heart! heart! heart!.... O Captain! my Captain! rise up and hear the bells; Rise up--for you the flag is flung--for you the bugle trills; For you bouquets and ribbon'd wreaths--for you the shores a-crowding; For you they call, the swaying mass, their eager faces turning; Here Captain! dear father!....
The ship is anchor'd safe and sound, its voyage closed and done; From fearful trip, the victor ship, comes in with object won;...

text: The growing industry awareness of air quality and emissions in the world's ports could be a catalyst for major change in the bunker market. In the next few weeks the International Maritime Organization (IMO) is expected to meet and try to reach some agreement on both the specification of marine fuels and standards to be imposed. This issue has been hotly contested among shipowners and refiners as these parties can expect to bear the brunt of any increased costs that may result from higher spec fuels. With bunker prices already substantially higher than where they were even a year ago, shipowners seem justified in being jittery about a further price increases. The chart below shows the average price of bunker fuels, Intermediate Fuel Oil 380 (CST) and Marine Diesel Oil (MDO). MDO prices in some markets topped $1,000 per metric ton this week, perhaps a sign of shrinking availability of supplies.

Currently, there are just a few areas that have taken aggressive steps toward limiting emissions. The Sulfur Emission Control Area (SECA) in the Baltic and Northwest Europe are setting an example for other environmentally sensitive, highly trafficked ports. Ships are required to burn low-sulfur fuels while in these controlled waters and can switch back to regular sulfur contents once outside.
The likely outcome of the IMO meeting will be proposals that address the bunker emissions on a worldwide basis. Some of the suggested proposals have been as broad based as 1.00% sulfur content worldwide by 2012, with further reductions to 0.50% by 2015. Other proposals involve more lax global standards, but with a more aggressive implementation timeline for SECA zones. Restrictions on what fuels shippers can burn will create more competition for the quantities and qualities refiners are able to produce, sustaining the environment for upward price pressures.

With the expected growth of seaborne trade worldwide, an expanding market for bunkers is expected. While in general this demand is expected to grow, the availability of suitable supply could be a mounting concern. There are worries that higher costs could be incurred as refiners have to upgrade facilities in order to produce the bunker fuels with the acceptable sulfur content.
There has been talk of pushing the industry toward a greater use of distillate fuel; a feat that many believe to be impractical. With distillate prices almost 70% higher than where they were a year ago, it is hard to create the incentive for shipowners to make the switch. There is also fear that there is not enough capacity to produce the amount of distillate that would be required as bunkers.
As bunker demand grows, prices will probably increase as well. With this, there will likely be economic incentives for refiners to work toward optimizing their production of marine fuels to meet growing demand. In the near-term, however, it is hard to see what forces would weaken bunker prices appreciably.

As the oil company executives (and several well informed Members of Congress) pointed out, the main cause for record high gasoline prices is record high crude prices: WTI crude prices have been consistently above $100 per barrel and have even reached $110 per barrel on occasion over the last month. In fact, the R-Squared correlation between gasoline prices and crude prices from Jan 2000 to the present has been 91%. The below graphic from the US Government's own EIA website shows the components of the February 2008 gasoline price. After crude oil, which comprised nearly 70% of the gasoline price, the next largest component was taxes, followed by distribution and marketing costs, and also refining costs. At current levels of $3.29 per gallon gasoline and $106 per barrel WTI, crude comprises 77% of the current gasoline price.
Members of the special House Committee recommended several steps to lower gasoline prices, including forcing big oil companies to pledge 10% of profits to renewable energy, supporting legislation to promote energy independence, and ceasing the filling of the SPR. Unfortunately, vague legislation to promote energy independence won't likely fix the problem; equally, ceasing to fill the SPR, which has increased by approximately 1 million barrels over the last month (equal to approximately 0.2% of US consumption over that period) will not likely lower gasoline prices. Nor will diverting profits to renewable energy abet the problem: renewable energy investment does not immediately lower gasoline prices. Nor does such investment address the main structural hindrance to growth for both renewable and fossil fuel energy: a lack of sufficient infrastructure to engage projects. Just as wind power companies cannot get turbine blades quickly enough, oil companies cannot quickly lease or acquire the offshore rigs they require to drill in deepwater.
These suggestions to lower gasoline prices highlight a systemic problem: the proposed solutions do not address the problem at hand. How will pumping money into renewables and "promoting energy independence" lower pump prices in the short term? No matter whether one believes in the future of renewable energies, pumping billions of dollars into these efforts now will not produce immediately lower gasoline prices.

According to the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) some of the objectives of the expansion are to maintain the Canal's competitiveness as a viable maritime route and increase Canal payments to the National Treasury. The payments to the National Treasury are derived in three ways: on a per net ton basis, as a payment for public services and as a payment based on Canal operations. In 2005, the total amount of these direct payments from the Canal to the National Treasury amounted to $489 million. This number is expected to triple by 2015. Delays for the canal have proven to be a 'choke point' for tanker owners in recent months. Currently delays at the Canal can amount to almost a full week, increasing the costs to charterers. In early April, the ACP created an auction for one additional booking slot per day, with the expectation that the price for this slot would open at around $35,000. In fact, slot prices have ranged between $65,000 to $150,000 per crossing. The rapid increase in bidding for the slots is driven primarily by competition from other vessel sectors, specifically reefers, whose cargo is time sensitive.
The amount of delays serves as an indication to the maritime community that there is a need for more capacity in the Canal. Assessment It is clear that widening the Canal will improve the traffic flow in the region. However, there is also a strong possibility that overtime the structural changes will open the Canal to more traffic overall, largely from container vessels which could further complicate traffic patterns. Improved traffic conditions will change the way crude and products are parceled and shipped between the Atlantic and Pacific. If the opposite conditions arise and delays worsen due to increased traffic charterers could stand to be paying even more in demurrage. Could VLCCs someday transit the canal? That would be some plan.

text: In a huge upset, it was recently announced that sales of Ford's dominant F-series truck lagged smaller, more fuel efficient cars like the Honda Civic and Accord, and the Toyota Camry and Corolla. In fact, the Ford F-series's fifth place showing in May 2008 US auto sales data marks the first time these trucks have failed to hold onto the top spot since June 2005 (when another truck briefly topped it). Ford sold just under 43,000 F-series trucks in May 2008, a 30% drop from May 2007. The graph below shows US gasoline consumption since 2000. Though the overall trend has been increasing overall consumption, it is clear that change is coming. With gasoline at $4+/gallon, consumers' driving habits appear to be changing to more car pooling, public transportation, and of course the purchasing of more fuel efficient automobiles. The question is: how big of an impact will this vehicle sales shift actually have, and how will the tanker market be affected?

text: It would appear to the casual observer that this change in auto sale trends will significantly affect gasoline consumption and thus tanker demand. That supposition may only be half-right, however, if at all. If we take data on the top 10 best selling autos in the US in May 2008, we calculate a weighted average fuel economy of 27.9 miles per gallon. Compare that figure with the weighted average fuel economy of 24.2 miles per gallon for the top selling cars from full-year 2006, and it is clear that fuel economy is a more important factor in auto sales than in previous years. Further, reports indicate that auto sales in May 2008 were down 7.4% versus the prior year, to 1.4 million vehicles. If we assume that each vessel drives approximately 15,000 miles per year, indicative annual gasoline consumption for May 2008 vehicle purchases would be 752 million gallons, and 936 million gallons for May 2007 vehicle purchases. This 183 million gallon decline over a year certainly appears to be substantial. If we apply this analysis to tanker demand effects, though, we see that 183 million gallons represents 4.3 million barrels, or about 14 MR gasoline cargoes per year. In short, this volume change only represents lower MR demand of about 1 vessel per month. In addition, it is possible that the lowered gasoline consumption could equate to lower domestic refinery output, rather than reduced imports, so the net impact could be even less than 1 MR cargo per month. In fact, new auto sales may not actually replace other less efficient vehicles: they may represent new drivers, or may reflect the need to drive even more. So the net effect of the changing preference for more fuel economic vehicles may not actually bring down gasoline consumption in the short term. The recent shift in consumer preferences towards more fuel efficient vehicles is a major development that should significantly impact gasoline consumption over the long term. Over the short term, however, the net effect is actually quite small, and even smaller for the tanker market: demand remains high.

text:
To give some perspective on the many intertwined factors that continue to push oil's price to ever loftier levels, Michael D. Tusiani, Chairman and CEO of Poten & Partners, shared his views of not only these factors, but also of what should be done to mitigate them with Lloyd's List readers earlier this week. The article that follows captures the full essence of what was published by Lloyd's List on June 9th.
Why Is The Oil Price High And What Can Be Done About It?
The primary reason the price of oil is high is that America's political leaders, for individual gain and popularity, have failed to enact a coherent and effective energy policy. They have acted irresponsibly by avoiding addressing the problem of increasing global demand and lagging supply and by lacking the resolve to establish measures to curb demand and waste. Americans are just beginning to suffer the consequences of such poor leadership.
The other reason is financial speculation which is being fueled by inconsistent government actions. Increasing Global Demand and Lagging Supply Rhetoric notwithstanding, there are no viable substitutes for transportation fuels such as gasoline and jet fuel for at least the next few decades. In addition to the rapidly increasing demand from China, India and other countries eager to grow and improve their living standards, there is also continued demand growth from developed markets such as the United States. Economic growth is not possible without increasing energy supplies.
Producing countries are not withholding oil from the market. Quite to the contrary, they are supplying the quantities requested by their customers. This is evidenced by the fact that ships are not delayed at load ports. Fifteen years ago the world had the benefit of roughly 9 million barrels per day of spare crude oil producing capacity. Today that surplus has been reduced dramatically, probably to no more than 3 million barrels per day. At that same time, refining capacity was also in surplus. Although existing refineries have been expanded, no new ones have been built in the developed world. And, as an added complication, because of the differences in product specifications, certain crude oils can only be processed at specific refineries. Thus, any headline event, such as a temporary loss of supply, a natural disaster or a weather calamity, has a magnified impact on oil price levels. In addition, the easily accessible oil has been found and new supplies, much of them located in politically difficult geographies, will be very costly and complex to bring to market. Price volatility is high.

In recent months, in order to demonstrate their willingness to combat the high price of oil, some legislators have been suggesting some rather nonsensical solutions such as a summer moratorium on the federal gas tax; a windfall profit tax on oil companies; a clampdown on futures trading; an attempt to claim that OPEC is an illegal monopoly under US Law; halting the approvals of military sales to Saudi Arabia, etc. These efforts are only detracting from the actions that need to be taken.
In the short term, the U.S. Government should: tighten CAFE standards for trucks and other light vehicles used for normal transportation; eliminate ethanol tariffs so that imports can displace domestic production to reduce pressure on corn and other grain prices; turn down heating and cooling systems; unitize product quality standards across the country. Although the intended purpose of a petroleum stockpile is not to manipulate price, if only for psychological reasons, the willingness to provide a short-term supply jolt may be necessary in today's market environment as an expedient measure to introduce downside risks for speculative players. Therefore, the Administration should not only temporarily halt the purchase of oil for storage to demonstrate that it is unwilling to buy regardless of price but, in conjunction with the EU, Japan and some farsighted OPEC producers, be prepared to release specific volumes of crude and products into the market as circumstances warrant. Although these solutions have been proposed in the past, today's circumstances make each of these actions critically important.
In the long term, obvious actions should be pursued. Our Government must encourage the development of oil and gas resources (for which there are no foreseeable substitutes). But, also incentivize research in alternative energy technologies such as carbon capture to allow the increased use of domestic coal. In addition, facilitate the construction of new nuclear power capacity and the improvement of infrastructure to allow the United States to import the energy it needs more safely and economically. Reform product quality regulations to set performance standards rather than mandate product components such as ethanol use in gasoline. Improve construction standards for buildings and factories to encourage more efficient energy usage. Accelerate modern air and ground traffic control systems to halt the waste of aviation fuels. Finally, we must restore the integrity of the U.S. dollar.
The time has come for us to act sensibly. Today's high oil price may be a blessing in disguise. It affords our political leaders the opportunity to admit and rectify their mistakes of the past.

There is an estimated 45 billion barrels of oil in the US Gulf of Mexico between the Western, Central and Eastern Planning Areas. Production is generally categorized as follows: shallow water is less that 1,000 feet, deep water is between 1,000 and 7,500 feet and ultra-deep water is greater than 7,500 feet. While development in shallower water permits the use of fixed structures, there is increasing use of floating structures, such as Floating Production Storage and Offloading (FPSO) units, as the production moves toward deep and ultra-deep water.
After the exploration and decision to produce is made, field operators and partners must choose which topside unit - spars, semi- submersible units, disconnectable floating units (FPUs), or FPSO - to employ. This decision will coincide with the choice between pipeline or shuttle tanker for crude oil transportation to shore.
There are several considerations to take into account when choosing between shuttle tankers and pipelines. Perhaps first and foremost is protection from the different crude oils mixing in the pipeline that can affect the crude oil integrity and the ability to market the oil to more than one discharge location. Weather can be another factor to consider; the affects of hurricanes on fixed structures in the US Gulf of Mexico has been well documented. However fog and other weather delays must be taken into account. The ability to tie into existing pipeline infrastructure, due to distance, underlying terrain, or material constraints such as pipeline capacity, may prove to be other hurdles in the near term for new field production.
Perhaps the most interesting field development from a shipping perspective has been the Cascade-Chinook fields, in the Walker Ridge, that is lead by Petrobras. The company drew on their existing FPSO and shuttle tanker expertise in other parts of the world to become 'first movers' on the use of shuttle tankers in the US Gulf. By teaming up with experienced and quality operators for the FPSO and shuttle tankers, the company concluded that shuttle tankers would provide, safe, reliable and cost-effective transportation for crude oil.
Going-forward expect more companies to follow the lead of Petrobras. The use of the FPSO and shuttle tanker model is expected to grow in the US Gulf. In fact, as more operators adopt the system, the unit transportation cost of crude oil can be better optimized as vessels can improve their utilization by trading among different fields.

Producers, traders, brokers, buyers, regulators and financiers gathered this June in Houston at Platts 5 th annual Bunker & Residual Fuel Oil Conference to hear other industry players' views of what the future holds for the "bottom of the barrel" oils. All of the presentations outlined the general notion that the fuel oil industry grapples with fast- changing developments such as heavier crude slates, refinery upgrades, decline in consumption by the electricity and manufacturing industries, and fuel oil quality modifications reflecting increasing environmental concerns.
To give some perspective on the direction marine fuel regulations are headed, Stefka Ilieva, a fuel oil analyst and editor of Poten's monthly publication Fuel Oil in World Markets , was invited as a panel speaker to share her views on the impact of the International Maritime Organization's (IMO) bunker fuel standards on bunker production as well as possible solutions. The following is an outline of the presentation given in Houston on June 24 th . IMO's Alphabet Soup The Marine Environmental Protection Committee (MEPC), one of five IMO committees, introduced a maritime pollution convention - MARPOL back in the 1970's. MARPOL is currently comprised of six Annexes. Annex VI: Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships, is aimed at reducing harmful sulfur oxides emissions from ships by restricting the sulfur content of bunker fuels. It entered into force on May 19, 2005 by establishing a worldwide sulfur cap of 4.5 percent. In 2006 and 2007 Annex VI went on to create two Sulfur Emissions Control Areas (SECAs) in the Baltic Sea and the North Sea/English Channel limiting marine fuel sulfur to 1.5 percent. The MEPC is meeting this October to possibly adopt further proposed global and SECA restrictions.

On October 3, 2008, the United States House of Representatives passed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 (the "Stabilization Act" or "Act").
1 The Senate had already passed the Stabilization Act on October 1, 2008. The Stabilization Act is only part of a much larger bill that contains various tax and other provisions. The Stabilization Act aims to provide stability to the US financial system by eliminating uncertainty regarding the value of mortgage-related financial instruments, restoring confidence among financial institutions regarding this aspect of their mutual viability as trading partners and reopening the market for the credit and other financial transactions that the US economy depends on. The principal difference between this version of the Act and that which originally failed to pass the House is the addition of a temporary increase in the amount of deposit insurance and the addition of a large number of unrelated tax provisions. This Client Alert discusses only the principal elements of the Stabilization Act that relate to the current financial crisis.
Overview . Fundamentally, the Stabilization Act: Authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to establish programs to either purchase or guarantee mortgage-related assets; Defines the institutions and asset types eligible to participate in these programs; Provides for up to $700 billion to be made available for these programs, but only in tranches, subject to various approval procedures; 1 The full text of the legislation may be found at http://financialservices.house.gov/essa/essabill.pdf and the House Financial Services Committee's section-by-section summary may be found at http://financialservices.house.gov/essa/eesabill_section-by-section.pdf .

Eligible Institutions . The Stabilization Act applies to institutions established and regulated under the laws of the United States and the states, commonwealths and territories. The word "established" means that US branches and agencies of international institutions are covered, so long as these branches and agencies are regulated in the US and have "significant operations in" the US. The Act states that these institutions include, but are not limited to, banks, savings associations, credit unions, securities brokers and dealers, and insurance companies. Although the Act uses the term "financial institution," it does not specify what kinds of activities are "financial" or what constitutes "regulation."
Eligible Assets . Eligible assets consist of all types of mortgages and securities, obligations and instruments "based on or related to" all types of mortgages, so long as the mortgages, securities, obligations or instruments were "originated or issued" on or before March 14, 2008 ("Troubled Assets"). The Act contains additional authority for the purchase of any other financial instrument if the purchase is determined to be necessary to promote financial market stability.

In addition, if it uses its purchase authority, it must also establish a program to make available guarantees of up to 100 percent of the value of any Troubled Assets. As part of guaranteeing assets, Treasury must charge the institution being assisted a premium "in an amount that the Secretary determines necessary to meet the purposes of [the] Act and to provide sufficient reserves" to meet anticipated (actuarially determined) claims and protect taxpayers. The authority of the Treasury and the Office of Financial Stability is broad and would appear to offer the possibility of creating numerous innovative structures to protect both financial institutions and shareholders. The Stabilization Act provides authority for the Treasury to manage assets it acquires. This authority appears to be applicable to both the purchase and the guarantee programs and should assist in making innovative structures possible. It is unclear what the effect of Section 106(d) might be on the ability to craft its proposals. That section requires Treasury to transfer the revenues and proceeds of Troubled Assets it acquires to the Treasury's general fund for the reduction of the public debt.
Amounts Available . Initially, the Treasury's purchase authority is limited to $250 billion. This limitation and the other purchase authority limits set forth in the Act are reduced by an amount equal to the difference between the outstanding guarantees and the balance in the fund that contains the "fees" (presumably, the premiums) collect under the guarantee program. The reference to the balance presumably means that premiums and other amounts to be collected in the future cannot be counted until received.The Treasury's purchase authority can be increased to $350 billion by the President at any time and up to $700 billion by the President acting with Congress. Congress may also block the exercise of purchase authority in excess of $350 billion. Interestingly, the dollar limitation on the Treasury's purchase authority is phrased in terms of amounts "outstanding at any one time," which perhaps means that Treasury's authority is like a revolving line of credit.
Transparency and Supervision . The Comptroller General will have oversight over the program established by the Treasury and must issue reports at least every 60 days. Annual audits are required, as is an effective system of internal control, such as that required by Sarbanes-Oxley.

New executive compensation and corporate governance standards will apply to financial institutions that sell Troubled Assets directly to the Treasury and issue to the Treasury in the transaction meaningful equity or debt positions. text: In an effort to head off a potential collapse in the oil market, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) has moved their November meeting ahead to next week. The market has already begun to speculate that the general softening in crude oil prices means a cut in production is afoot. Member countries are to decide whether increasing, decreasing or leaving production levels unchanged will be most beneficial to market stabilization in the coming months. By controlling such a large degree of both upstream production and spare capacity in the marketplace, decisions made by OPEC can have a potentially widespread impact on crude oil supply and in turn prices.

While it is sometimes difficult to determine the root causes of the bursts in the market, a downward correction in freight rates can be felt quickly especially if there is a surplus of tonnage. Sudden changes in demand and consumption patterns can convert a well supplied market into one with a capacity glut to the detriment of shipowners. Various shipping sectors - tankers, containers, dry bulk, and gas - will experience peaks and troughs at different points for a variety of reasons and durations. It appears that dry bulk shipping has fallen victim to a few of the classic symptoms of a market bubble. Demand for dry bulk commodities grew creating congestion at ports with insufficient infrastructure. Delays helped to further tighten supply in the market as ships were forced to wait longer to load and discharge cargoes. Add in the fact that freight rates escalated as charters were arranged back-to- back and ships were flipped among different charterers. As credit tightened, these pressures rapidly unwound to reveal lower charter rates combined with a dearth of cargoes in the market.
It stands to reason that the physical demand for commodities still remains in the dry bulk sector; however the pop in the bulker shipping bubble has created some unwarranted jitters rippling across the tanker market. The characteristics confronting the dry bulk market could potentially develop in other shipping sectors, however the tanker market seems to have different fundamentals to help insulate from insolvency.

Consider the gain on a 2 million barrel cargo and the charterer could effectively gross $1.6 million. Certainly other costs will be a limiting factor on the gross spread, such as bunkers used during the storage period, insurance and cargo loss.
